book.title: Z80: The Amazing Processor of the 1970s

sections.title: A World of Wire and Iron
sections.content:
Imagine an engineer in 1968. Not a purchasing manager, not an accountant — a design engineer sitting at a desk covered in component catalogs. His mission: to build the controller for a new factory machine. A system for automated counting and packaging, let's say.

Until yesterday, the previous version of this machine had been built with hundreds of TTL chips and thousands of hand-soldered wires. Today, the factory manager has issued a new order: the new machine must be twice as fast, have more memory, and print a daily report. Our engineer looks at the design he drew up last month, and he knows — he has to start over from scratch. The old board is useless now. Hardwired logic, like lines carved into stone, cannot be changed. He must design a new board, with a fresh arrangement of chips — and if a new requirement arises tomorrow, this board, too, will be thrown onto the scrap heap of history.

This was the true nightmare of the electronics industry in the 1960s: disposable logic. Every new product demanded new hardware. Every small change in function meant redesigning the printed circuit board, rewiring everything, and months of testing. The cost of designing custom hardware for every single application was a boulder chained to the ankle of innovation.

On a larger scale, the manufacturers of big computers were struggling with another version of the same disease. Every new model from DEC or IBM had its own unique internal architecture. But their main problem wasn't software incompatibility — that was the customer's headache, not the manufacturer's. The manufacturers' own problem was exactly the same as that of the factory controller engineer: designing new hardware for every generation, on a massive scale, at staggering cost. Locking the customer into a closed ecosystem was a side effect of this situation — not the root cause.

Inside Fairchild Semiconductor, a spark was forming. A young engineer named Ted Hoff, working on memory chip designs, had grown sick of this vicious cycle. In conversation with his colleague Stanley Mazor, he floated an idea that, at first glance, seemed almost naive: "Why scatter the logic of computation across dozens of chips? Why not gather all of it into a single chip? A central chip that could play the role of a brain for any device, simply by executing different instructions?"

Hoff's idea was to separate "operational logic" from "physical hardware." Instead of designing a dedicated electronic board with fixed wiring for every product, a standard chip could play any role by reading instructions stored in memory. Today, a packaging controller. Tomorrow, a calculator. The day after, a fire alarm system. The hardware stayed the same; it was the software that changed.

The idea went nowhere at Fairchild. But fate had other plans.

In 1969, a Japanese company named Busicom approached Intel — which had just broken away from Fairchild — with an order to design a set of twelve custom chips for an advanced desktop calculator. Ted Hoff, now at Intel, instead of following the original plan, made Busicom a revolutionary counterproposal: instead of twelve chips, let's design four. Let one of them be a central processing unit that handles all the calculations. By changing the program stored in memory, the same hardware could perform entirely different tasks.

Busicom's managers, after a brief hesitation, agreed. And so the work began.

Hoff and Mazor designed the logical architecture on paper. But turning this design into an actual chip on silicon was a task bordering on miracle. This is where two decisive figures entered the story: Federico Faggin, an Italian engineer who had just joined Intel and was a peerless master of physical chip design; and Masatoshi Shima, a Japanese engineer from Busicom who implemented the digital logic with obsessive precision. Faggin would later say: "Without Shima, the 4004 would never have been built." It was this four-man team — Hoff, Mazor, Shima, and Faggin — who brought the world's first commercial microprocessor into existence.

On November 15, 1971, Intel introduced the 4004: a 4-bit chip with 2,300 transistors. On the surface, it was just a faster brain for advanced calculators. But beneath the surface, it carried a revolutionary concept: universal programmable control. For the first time, "what a device does" had been separated from "how it is physically wired."

In the months that followed, creative engineers in corners of the world began discovering this concept. In major cities, traffic light controllers — once cabinets full of relays and wires — were now running on a single 4004 and a memory chip. Changing the traffic pattern no longer required dispatching an engineering team for rewiring; you simply swapped the memory chip for one with the new program. A quiet, invisible revolution was unfolding inside medical devices, industrial controllers, and security systems.

sections.title: A Bridge to the Personal Computer
sections.content:
The 4004 had one fundamental limitation: it processed only 4 bits per cycle. In a world where the standard for text processing was 8-bit ASCII codes, this was like walking on one leg. The industry needed a processor that could handle a full "byte" in a single pass.

Intel answered in April 1972 with the 8008: the world's first 8-bit microprocessor. The story of the 8008's birth held an important lesson. A company called CTC (later DataPoint) wanted to build a desktop computer for small businesses: the DataPoint 2200. They approached Intel to design the processor, and their requirements directly shaped the 8008's architecture. Intel built the 8008 to be the beating heart of that computer.

But fate, once again, charted a different course. The first 8008 samples arrived late, and their performance — due to the use of slow PMOS technology — was unsatisfactory. The engineers at CTC, tired of waiting, built their machine using around a hundred discrete TTL chips and set the 8008 aside. Thus, the first attempt to build a personal computer around a microprocessor ended in relative failure.

But the 8008 taught the industry an enormous lesson: an 8-bit microprocessor could, conceptually, serve as the core of a complete computer. The path was now open.

The lessons of the 4004 and the 8008 — one a triumph, the other a near-failure — led Intel to design a processor that would change everything. In April 1974, Intel brought the 8080 to market: faster NMOS technology, a clock speed of 2 megahertz, and a rich instruction set. But the true genius of the 8080 was not in its hardware; it was in Intel's open approach. They published complete documentation and explicitly invited other companies to build compatible peripheral chips. This move created a vast market of memory chips, controllers, and I/O ports — all revolving around the 8080.

The fruit of this open ecosystem ripened in January 1975. Popular Electronics magazine revealed a device on its cover called the Altair 8800: a computer based on the 8080, offered as a kit for $439. The reaction was beyond anything imagined. Tens of thousands of orders poured in from engineers, students, and hobbyists who had never before had access to a computer.

The Altair became the birthplace of a social movement. In garages and basements, users built hardware for it and shared their designs in magazines like BYTE. Two young students named Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote a BASIC interpreter for the Altair — and this became the foundation stone of a tiny company called Micro-Soft.

But the Altair's most important legacy was something Gary Kildall created. Kildall, a quiet university professor with a Ph.D. in computer science, wrote an operating system called CP/M. The genius of CP/M was this: a standard software layer that sat between application programs and different hardware. A programmer could write a word processor like WordStar once and be certain it would run on any machine with CP/M.

CP/M rapidly became the dominant standard for business computers. And this created an enormous strategic asset for the 8080 architecture: a vast library of business software that practically only ran on 8080-compatible processors. It was no longer hardware that sold the computer; it was software. Companies bought computers to run WordStar and VisiCalc. Any processor that wanted to be taken seriously in the market had to conquer this software territory.

sections.title: A Different Vision — and a Rebellion from Pennsylvania
sections.content:
Just as the 8080 was conquering the market, a completely different vision emerged from Motorola: the 6800 processor. If the 8080 was the symbol of an open and sometimes chaotic ecosystem, the 6800 was the embodiment of order, integration, and engineering elegance.

Motorola's team, led by Tom Bennett — who had glimpsed the original idea from Ted Hoff — insisted on different principles. The 6800 needed only a single +5V power supply, whereas the 8080 required three different voltages. This simplicity meant lower cost, higher reliability, and easier power supply design. The 6800's internal architecture was also symmetric and logical, making assembly-language programming intuitive and less error-prone. But most importantly, Motorola took a "system on a chip" approach: they introduced the 6800 not as a standalone chip, but as the central core of the "M6800 family" — a complete set of memory and interface chips that worked together naturally.

Federico Faggin, the architect of the 8080, admitted with respect: "The 6800 has a better architecture. It's a cleaner machine."

But the 6800 had two weak points: a higher price, and the absence of the enormous software ecosystem the 8080 had inherited through CP/M. Motorola never conquered the personal computer market, but it remained unrivaled elsewhere: industry. Point-of-sale terminals, early ATMs, and industrial controllers — places where durability and reliability mattered more than raw processing power — became the unchallenged domain of the 6800.

The market now had two powerful poles: Intel, with a vast software ecosystem but relatively complex hardware; and Motorola, with a beautiful, integrated design that was expensive and lacked business software. It was as if the industry was waiting for a synthesis of the two.

But before that could happen, an earthquake from Pennsylvania caught everyone off guard.

Chuck Peddle, a self-taught engineer and former soldier with a rebellious spirit, had been one of the 6800's designers at Motorola. When Motorola's management kept the 6800's price high, Peddle could not bear it. He told his colleague Bill Mensch: "These people think a processor is a luxury item. But I know it's the foundation stone of the future. It needs to be so cheap that any school student can buy one."

In the spring of 1974, Peddle and Mensch left Motorola and joined a small, obscure company called MOS Technology in Pennsylvania. There, in a windowless room, on a shoestring budget, they began to work. Peddle led brainstorming sessions with shouts: "Cut this section! What does the customer really want? Cheapness and efficiency!" Mensch, silent and focused, drew the new architecture on paper using the absolute minimum of transistors.

The result was unveiled in September 1975 at the Atlantic City exhibition: the MOS 6502. The price? Twenty-five dollars. While the 8080 cost about $175.

A wave of shock, and then excitement, swept through the hall. Young engineers surrounded the MOS booth. One of them was Steve Wozniak, who bought several samples and, in his father's garage, built a computer with one. His friend Steve Jobs insisted they sell it. They called it the Apple I — and this was the spark that built Apple. Later, Commodore placed the 6502 at the heart of the best-selling personal computer in history, the Commodore 64, and into the Atari 2600 game console.

Peddle had proven that a low price was itself a form of power. But the 6502 was not compatible with the 8080 — this processor belonged to a parallel world, the world of consumers and games, not the CP/M-dominated business market. Kildall's software empire remained untouched.

sections.title: Coup in the Shadows
sections.content:
In Federico Faggin's office at Intel, the atmosphere was heavy. He was the architect of the 4004 and the 8080, a man with silicon dust flowing through his veins. He had come from Italy to live the dream of building integrated circuits, and now his greatest achievement — the 8080 — had conquered the market.

But Intel's management, led by Gordon Moore and Andy Grove, saw the future differently. Their strategy was focused on semiconductor memories, and they regarded the microprocessor as a side activity. They refused to invest seriously in the next generation.

Faggin was furious at this shortsightedness. In the autumn of 1974, he made his decision. He went to Ralph Ungermann, a clever and ambitious executive, and in a simple restaurant in Palo Alto, he said: "Ralph, we are building the future, but they only see the past. I want to build a company focused on one thing and one thing only: building the best microprocessor in the world. Not good — the best."

Ungermann agreed. With investment from the oil company Exxon, Zilog was founded in November 1974. The name came from "Z-integrated logic," and Z — the last letter of the alphabet — seemed to signal a determination to build the last, the ultimate processor.

But Faggin was not alone. He went to Masatoshi Shima. Shima, the brilliant Japanese engineer who had worked alongside Faggin to build the 8080's architecture, was now back in Japan. Faggin sat across from him in a Japanese restaurant and, without preamble, said: "Shima-san, we want to finish what we started with the 8080. A processor that is not only better than the 8080 — but better than anything that exists. You must come with us." Shima, without a moment's hesitation, bowed his head in assent.

The golden circle was complete: Faggin, Shima, and Ungermann. Three men with three complementary forces: vision, precision, and management. They gathered in Zilog's small office in Cupertino and wrote down three principles that would alter the course of history:

1. Full compatibility: The new processor must be binary-compatible with the 8080. The entire CP/M software empire — WordStar, dBASE, and whatever came next — had to run on the new chip without the slightest change. This was an inheritance that could not be ignored.
2. Absolute superiority: They must not simply build a faster 8080. They had to improve on everything: more registers, more powerful instructions, higher speed, and — the great lesson of the 6800 — a single +5V supply. The new processor had to combine the best of both worlds: the ecosystem power of the 8080, and the engineering elegance of the 6800.
3. A price to shock the market: Not so low that they entered a futile war with the 6502 in the consumer market (the CP/M business market was the target, not game consoles), but competitive enough to tempt customers of Intel's 8080 and 8085 to migrate.

The year 1976 began. On the surface, everything in the industry appeared calm. Intel was working on the 8085 — an attempt to bring single-voltage supply to the 8080 architecture, designed precisely to counter the 6800's advantage. Motorola still relied on its elegant but expensive 6800. MOS was tearing through the consumer market with the 6502. And the CP/M empire, with unshakeable loyalty to the 8080 architecture, ruled the world of business software.

But in Zilog's office, the silence meant nothing but pure concentration. Faggin and Shima bent over silicon layouts day and night. They had only one chance, and they knew it.

On a spring evening in March 1976, Faggin finished his final review. He rose from his desk, walked to the window, and stared at the quiet street beyond the glass. Then, turning to Shima and his small team, he said with the calm that comes from certainty: "It's done. We have it."

He paused, and then, his voice slightly louder: "Now they must know that a new king has arrived."

The Z80 was now born. And nothing would ever be the same again.
